lists-intro.title: Coding exercise: build a shopping list
lists-intro.prompt: Add three items to the groceries list, then print its length.

motivation.body: Imagine tracking a shopping list, a class roster, or your top five songs — you need somewhere to hold many values together, in order. That's exactly what a list does.

explanation.body: A list is an ordered collection of values, written with square brackets and separated by commas. You can access any item by its position (its index), starting from 0.

illustration.caption: Each item in a list sits in a numbered box, starting at index 0 — not 1.

video.title: Lists in 4 minutes
video.comingSoon: Video lessons are being produced — check back soon.

examples.note: append() adds one item to the end.
len() tells you how many items are in the list.
Negative indices count from the end — -1 is the last item.

steps: Add a second task the same way.
Print todo to see both tasks together.

quiz.question: What will print(len(["a", "b", "c"])) output?
quiz.explanation: len() counts the items in the list — there are three: "a", "b", and "c".

challenge.prompt: Build a playlist: create a list of 3 song titles, add a 4th with append(), then print how many songs are in the playlist.
challenge.starterCode:
playlist = ["Song A", "Song B", "Song C"]
# add a 4th song below

print(len(playlist))

miniProject.title: Shopping List Manager
miniProject.brief: Extend today's groceries list into a tiny program: let it hold at least 5 items, remove one you no longer need with .remove(), and print the final list and its length.
miniProject.note: Full project submission and review tools are coming in a later update — for now, try this in the coding exercise above.

points: A list holds multiple values in order, written with square brackets.
Access items by index, starting at 0 — and -1 for the last item.
append() adds an item to the end; len() counts the items.

items.title: Off-by-one errors
items.body: Remember indices start at 0, so the third item is my_list[2], not my_list[3].

items.title: Forgetting append() returns nothing
items.body: my_list = my_list.append(x) sets my_list to None — just call my_list.append(x) on its own line.

items: Give lists plural, descriptive names like groceries or scores, not data or list1.
Use len(my_list) instead of counting manually — it stays correct as the list changes.
